extracted.intended_audience: scientists, journal editors, research-integrity professionals, and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Detecting, evaluating, and responding to doctored or manipulated images in academic research papers using a mix of image-forensics software and human investigation. Covers signals of manipulation, workflow options for journals/institutions, and limits of automated approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types/forms of image falsification to check for
rubrics_metrics.description: Image falsification can involve microscopic views of materials, cells, tissues, gel bands representing concentrations, or images of graphs based on research data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that many kinds of images are vulnerable — microscopy images, gel electrophoresis bands, graphs, and other visual data can be manipulated. Screening programs should include all common scientific image types rather than focusing on only one modality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplicated panels representing distinct samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Detect duplicated panels in the same figure that are purported to represent two distinct anatomical sites or different experimental conditions (e.g., '2 duplicated panels in the same figure, representing two distinct anatomical sites').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such duplications 'look like an error' but can be grounds for correction or retraction if deliberate; examples (Elisabeth Bik tweets) show how visual inspection or software can flag these cases for follow-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identical or eerily similar graphs across different experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag cases where graphs from different experiments or with wildly different concentrations appear eerily identical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated detection of identical graph shapes across supposedly different conditions (as in the homeopathy paper case) is a strong red flag. Follow-up should determine whether the duplication is a plotting error, reuse, or deliberate fabrication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pixel-level and structural manipulation signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Look for signals such as rotated parts, changed colors, and inappropriate reuse of image regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Image-forensics software commonly searches for rotated fragments, color edits, reuse of subregions, and other anomalies. These features are useful signals but require contextual evaluation to infer intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: duplication across large databases (cross-paper reuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare an image against a large database of articles to detect reuse of images across different papers — analogous to Turnitin for text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-scale comparisons enable detection of cross-paper reuse that manual inspection cannot scale to. Building or accessing a comprehensive image database is necessary for this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated flagging requires human verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Software output will have to be evaluated by a human; use of software does not eliminate the need for human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human evaluators reduce false positives and determine whether anomalies represent innocent errors, poor figure assembly, or intentional manipulation. The article emphasizes that human oversight remains essential even as software scales screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of false positives; verification reduces errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that automated methods can overflag; humans in the verification system help reduce false positives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use human review workflows to vet software hits. The article notes that scaling with software is essential for speed, but humans help filter spurious matches before action (corrections/retractions) is taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal pre-publication screening policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should consider screening images in incoming manuscripts, potentially using customized software tools or hired image analysts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The development of detection software 'has the potential to increase the number of journals that screen images.' Options include providing tools to editors or outsourcing checks to specialist companies or hired analysts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional capacity for investigation and prevention
rubrics_metrics.description: Public research institutions need resources both to face allegations against their researchers and to prevent misconduct by screening manuscripts prior to submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There will be demand for smaller businesses and single experts to provide screening services to institutions; institutions should build or buy access to expertise for internal investigations and preventative screening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of detection methods and results
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies using image-detection applications rarely publish their results, and press releases of busts based solely on software are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article implies that publishing methods and results increases accountability; reliance on opaque commercial tools without published evidence can leave uncertainty about validity of flags and conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for escalation (error vs intentional fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a detected anomaly is an error (e.g., figure assembly mistake) or intentional tampering before escalating to retraction or public accusation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes the distinction between anomalies and intentional fraud; software can report if tampering was likely intentional, but human evaluation is needed to decide on corrective actions like retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of scalable machine-learning approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Use machine-learning algorithms to crunch large numbers of papers and find suspicious images at scale (e.g., Acuna's algorithm finding ~9% suspicious images in a large scan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machine learning is necessary to scale comparisons across many papers and authors; it can identify candidates for human review but should be integrated into a workflow that includes verification and adjudication.
